title: Scottish Instruments — Traditional Voices I

blocks.text:
**Track:** regions | **Tier:** 2 | **Difficulty:** 4/10
**Prerequisites:** regions-celtic-scotland-01-overview
**Tags:** scotland, fiddle, pipes, whistle, harp, shetland, highland

This lesson examines five melody voices at the heart of Scottish traditional music: the **fiddle**, **Great Highland bagpipe**, **Scottish smallpipes**, **tin whistle**, and **clàrsach** (Scottish harp). Guidebooks often group them as "lead instruments," but session reality is messier — pipes supply harmonic drones, fiddle bowing drives ceilidh rhythm, and harp accompanies Gaelic song. Scottish trad shares ornament vocabulary with Ireland (cuts, rolls, snaps) yet regional accents — **Shetland**, **North East**, **West Highland** piping — sound unmistakably local.

Read alongside **Session Voices II**, which covers accordion, piano, guitar, and percussion in ceilidh bands and folk ensembles.

| Situation | What you might hear |
|-----------|---------------------|
| Ceilidh night | Fiddle and accordion on melody; pipes for a march set; whistle doubling the reel |
| Pipe band contest | Massed Highland pipes and drums only — no fiddle |
| Folk club | Smallpipes and harp on airs; whistle learner beside a seasoned fiddler |
| Shetland hall | Twin fiddles in ringing unison on reels unique to the islands |

**Who starts the tune** and **who matches whose phrasing** matter more than rigid "melody only" labels.

![Fiddler performing traditional music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Fiddle.jpg?width=640)

The **Scottish fiddle** is the violin played with traditional bowing, ornament, and repertoire centred on **reels**, **strathspeys**, **jigs**, and **slow airs**. **James Scott Skinner** (1843–1927), the "Strathspey King," composed and performed pieces that remain competition and session standards — *The Bonnie Lass of Bon Accord*, *Hector the Hero*. His Victorian showmanship bridged parlour taste and dance-hall drive.

sections.title: Regional schools: Shetland and North East

blocks.text:
**Shetland** fiddle style favours **ringing open strings**, precise ensemble with **twin fiddles**, and repertoire including **listening tunes** and Scandinavian-tinged melodies. Players like **Aly Bain** brought Shetland accent to international stages through **Boys of the Lough** and broadcasting. The **Shetland Folk Festival** concentrates island tradition for visitors and locals alike.

The **North East** (Aberdeenshire, Moray, Angus) produced fierce competition fiddlers and composers. **Scott Skinner** epitomises the region; modern players like **Paul Anderson** and **Alasdair Fraser** extend its technical brilliance. Bowing emphasises **strathspey snap** — the dotted long-short pulse that separates Scottish strathspeys from Irish reels.

**West Highland** and **Gaelic** areas may favour slower airs and pipe-influenced repertoire. **Cape Breton** fiddle in Nova Scotia preserves Scottish settler styles — a diaspora mirror worth comparing after you know mainland sources.

**James Scott Skinner** (1843–1927), the "Strathspey King," composed *The Bonnie Lass of Bon Accord* and *Hector the Hero* while touring as dancer and fiddler. His Victorian showmanship fixed strathspey repertoire for competition pipers and ceilidh bands alike. **Memorable detail:** Skinner marketed himself with photographs and composed pieces dedicated to patrons — trad entrepreneurship before the word "brand" dominated music.

**Aly Bain** (born 1946, Shetland) brought **ringing open-string** fiddle to television through *Boys of the Lough* and *Transatlantic Sessions*. His duets with Irish fiddlers model healthy cross-border listening. **Memorable detail:** Bain's bow arm favours **clarity over flash** — a Shetland lesson in ensemble discipline.

Shetland Fiddle tradition is among Scotland's most distinctive regional voices — not interchangeable with Sligo or Donegal accents.

Scottish fiddlers use **cuts**, **rolls**, **birls** (bowed tremolo figures), and **snap bowing** on strathspeys. Vibrato is sparing outside airs. **Scordatura** and **cross-tuning** appear in historical practice. Sessions and ceilidhs demand **danceable tempo** — flash without lift fails the room.

The **Great Highland bagpipe** (*pìob mhòr*) is mouth-blown, with a conical **chanter** and **drones** (bass, tenor, alto). Volume suits outdoors — games, parades, battle memorials. The chanter is **open-ended**; staccato comes from finger technique, not closed-end design like uilleann pipes.

**Pipe bands** layer multiple pipe chanters in unison with drum corps. Great Highland Bagpipe culture includes **solo piping competitions** at Highland games — **piobaireachd** (classical ceòl mòr) as well as march, strathspey, and reel sets.

Learners often begin on **practice chanter** before full pipes. Bag pressure from **mouth blowing** demands stamina; reeds need constant maintenance. In folk sessions, a lone piper may sit out crowded reels or lead a march set — etiquette parallels Irish pipe volume concerns.

![Bagpiper in traditional dress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Scottish_bagpiper_at_Pennsylvania_Renaissance_Faire.jpg?width=640)

**Scottish smallpipes** and **border pipes** are softer, often **mouth-blown** or **bellows-blown**, suited to **indoor** folk clubs and sessions. **Northumbrian** and **Border** traditions overlap the southern Scottish marches. Smallpipes let pipers join fiddle-and-accordion ceilidhs without overwhelming the room — parallel to uilleann pipes in Irish pubs, though mechanism and timbre differ.

Makers and players like **Hamish Moore** helped revive smallpipes for folk ensemble use in the late twentieth century. If Highland pipes are the national billboard, smallpipes are the **conversation voice** beside harp and whistle.

The **tin whistle** (*feadóg*) is inexpensive, portable, and widely taught in schools and folk workshops. In Scottish sessions it doubles fiddle melody at pitch or octave. Repertoire aligns with fiddle keys — **D**, **G**, **A** — with ornament (cuts, rolls, tonguing) matching Irish whistle technique closely enough that cross-border players swap tunes easily.

**Whistle** does not carry a distinct "Scottish only" reputation the way pipes do, but it remains a **gateway instrument** from childhood tuition to festival sessions. Listen for strathspey **articulation** — not every reel approach fits the snap.

The **clàrsach** is Scotland's historical wire- or gut-strung harp, cousin to the Irish **cláirseach**. Medieval **Gaelic** courts prized harpers; the **Queen Mary Harp** and **Lamont Harp** survive in museums as icons. Revival players — **Savourna Stevenson**, **Rachel Hair**, **Patsy Seddon** — perform dance tunes, airs, and song accompaniment.

Harp suits **folk clubs**, **Gaelic song** settings, and concert stages more than loud pub sessions. **Wire-strung** revivalists pursue bell-like historical timbre; **lever harps** handle modulations for modern ensemble work. Clàrsach connects Scotland to shared Gaelic harp heritage across the Irish Sea.

![Clàrsach (Scottish harp)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Clarsach.jpg?width=640)

Parallel lesson: `regions-celtic-ireland-02-instruments-voices-i`. Irish fiddle regions (Sligo, Donegal, Clare) differ from **Shetland** and **North East** Scottish schools, yet **Donegal** imports Scottish marches and strathspeys freely. **Uilleann pipes** are bellows-blown and indoor-voiced; **Great Highland pipes** are mouth-blown and outdoor-loud. Both nations share whistle and harp revival stories.

Irish sessions may lack pipe-band marches; Scottish ceilidhs may stack strathspey–reel–reel sets for dancers. Copy the **local accent** when you sit in — a Sligo roll on a strathspey snap will feel wrong under a Highland dancer's feet.

- **Shetland** and **North East** fiddle are flagship regional accents — learn them by name, not as generic "Scottish fiddle."
- **Great Highland bagpipe** dominates public image and pipe-band competition; **smallpipes** suit indoor folk ensemble.
- **Whistle** is a democratic session voice shared closely with Irish practice.
- **Clàrsach** links medieval Gaelic heritage to modern folk and song accompaniment.
- **James Scott Skinner** remains essential listening for strathspey repertoire and style.
- Instrument roles overlap — pipes drone, fiddle drives dance lift, harp accompanies song.

- **Mary Anne Alburger** — *Scottish Fiddlers and Their Music* (historical regional survey).
- **Joshua Dickson** — *When Piping Was Strong* (Highland piping tradition).
- **Wikipedia** — [Scottish fiddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_fiddle), [Great Highland bagpipe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Highland_bagpipe).
- **Shetland Folk Festival** and **Hands Up for Trad** websites for contemporary player discovery.

quiz_markdown:
### Q1. James Scott Skinner is widely known as:

- A) The Strathspey King — composer and virtuoso Scottish fiddler
- B) An Italian opera conductor only
- C) Inventor of the bodhrán tipper
- D) A Cape Breton accordion maker exclusively

**Answer:** A

### Q2. Shetland fiddle style is associated with ringing open strings and twin-fiddle ensemble tradition.

**Answer:** True

### Q3. Great Highland bagpipes are typically inflated by:

- A) Mouth blowing with bag under the arm
- B) Elbow bellows only like uilleann pipes
- C) Electric air compressor exclusively
- D) Foot pump operated by the dancer

**Answer:** A

### Q4. Scottish smallpipes are generally:

- A) Softer and more suitable for indoor folk sessions than massed Highland pipes
- B) Louder than a full pipe band on a games field
- C) Identical to Northumbrian pipes in every historical detail
- D) Never used with fiddle or whistle

**Answer:** A

### Q5. The clàrsach is:

- A) Scotland's traditional harp with medieval Gaelic heritage
- B) A type of snare drum in pipe bands
- C) An electronic keyboard from the 1980s
- D) A vocal technique for puirt à beul only

**Answer:** A

### Q6. Aly Bain is strongly associated with:

- A) Shetland fiddle and international folk broadcasting
- B) Flamenco guitar only
- C) Vienna waltz orchestra leadership
- D) Disco production in the 1970s

**Answer:** A

### Q7. Strathspey bowing on fiddle emphasises a dotted long-short pulse called the Scottish snap.

**Answer:** True

### Q8. Pipe bands at Highland games typically feature:

- A) Massed Great Highland bagpipes with drum corps
- B) Solo clàrsach with no other instruments
- C) Only jazz saxophone sections
- D) Synthesiser orchestration exclusively

**Answer:** A

### Q9. Tin whistle in Scottish trad shares much ornament technique with Irish whistle practice.

**Answer:** True

### Q10. North East Scotland fiddle tradition is linked to composers and players including Scott Skinner.

**Answer:** True

### Q11. Compared with Ireland, Great Highland pipes are generally louder and more associated with outdoor ceremonial and games contexts than uilleann pipes.

**Answer:** True

### Q12. Practice chanter is a common beginner step before playing full Highland bagpipes.

**Answer:** True
